newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian PM vows reforms but needs foreign investors.
newsitem.headline: Indian PM vows reforms but needs foreign investors.

text.p: Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda vowed on Thursday to press ahead with economic reforms, but said foreign investors needed to help overhaul India's ailing infrastructure and rich nations had to keep their markets open.

Deve Gowda told an international conference on the Asian economies that India's new budget, unveiled last week to the delight of financial markets, set a clear signal that the nation was committed to opening up to trade and investment.

"The recent budget sent a message that is categorically clear to the United States and to all other countries interested in coming to India -- our full cooperation will be there," Deve Gowda said. "There is no question of any doubts in the minds of investors."
Stock markets have piled on gains since Finance Minister P. Chidambaram proposed across-the-board tax cuts and import duty reductions in the budget for the year starting on April 1.
The prime minister said his government was interested in making the rupee fully convertible by scrapping remaining restrictions on some financial transactions.
"It is our intention to move towards full convertibility as early as possible," he said. "The reform process has to be widened and deepened to meet the challenges that remain."

The head of India's 15-party centre-left coalition which took power last June said the commitment to free-market reforms had outlived the change of governments at both the federal and state levels. "This clears the doubt for foreign investors."

But he said the major challenge ahead was to ensure adequate financing for core infrastructure sectors such as roads, ports, telecommunications and power to meet the needs of a growing economy. Enormous investments were needed, he said.
"They exceed not only the capacity of the government but of domestic savings. Inflows of foreign capital by necessity will have to play a major role in the development of infrastructure."
Deve Gowda said multilateral financial institutions must play a role by devising innovative packages.
"It would indeed be sad if the momentum of growth or the sustainability of reform in any of the developing countries is thwarted by the stranglehold of inadquate infrastructure."

International Monetary Fund managing director Michel Camdessus said on Wednesday that the first stage of economic reforms in India appeared to have lost some momentum, and bold new measures were needed.

Deve Gowda called on industrialised nations to ensure access to their markets for poor countries' goods and services, and to encourage the steady capital flows to meet growing investment needs and facilitate technology transfer.
Asked to compare India with China as regards foreign investment, Deve Gowda said India's independent judiciary protected investors' commitments.
He cited Enron Corp, which had a big power project in western India cancelled, then reinstated. "Ultimately, Mr Enron got justice. No investor will have any injustice in this country."
Deve Gowda then said to applause: "I don't want to compare ourselves with China. We are good friends."
